title: Magnonic cavity-enhanced quantum magnetometry with nitrogen-vacancy centre ensembles
abstract: Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centre ensembles are leading room-temperature magnetometers, but their sensitivity is usually extracted from a single resonance and relies on external microwave and bias-field hardware. This work proposes a chip-scale NV magnetometer built around a one-dimensional YIG/CoFeB magnonic crystal, in which a single structural defect forms a passive magnonic cavity and integrated permanent magnets supply the bias field. Micromagnetic simulations show a defect-localised spin-wave mode at 2.910 GHz inside the 2.5-3.0 GHz magnonic band gap, 40 MHz from the NV zero-field splitting, with a band structure that matches an independent plane-wave calculation. A Tavis-Cummings/Lindblad model in which the microwave reaches the NV ensemble through this mode predicts a hyperfine-resolved optically detected magnetic resonance spectrum that is strong only within the mode linewidth, and a dispersive homodyne response with one steep edge per $^{14}$N hyperfine line. The master-equation solutions agree with the closed-form homodyne steady state ($R^2 > 0.9999$) and with an approximate analytic ODMR theory (peak positions within 0.012 MHz). For a critically coupled readout with room-temperature electronics, combining the three edges gives a projected sensitivity of 93 pT/$\sqrt{\rm Hz}$, a $\sqrt{3}$-fold gain over the best single edge. Mapping the sensitivity against the NV-magnon coupling reveals an optimum near $g_{\rm ens}/2π\approx 0.2$-$0.4$ MHz, where it reaches 72 pT/$\sqrt{\rm Hz}$ for a 0.64 MHz spin linewidth and 19 pT/$\sqrt{\rm Hz}$ for 0.17 MHz, with thermal limits of 6.6 and 1.7 pT/$\sqrt{\rm Hz}$. The antenna-mode coupling, the NV-magnon coupling and the spin linewidth are therefore the main design levers.
summary: The authors propose a novel, chip-scale magnetometer using NV centers coupled to a defect-localized spin-wave mode in a magnonic crystal. By modeling the system dynamics using quantum master equations and analyzing the resulting homodyne response, they predict a substantial enhancement in magnetic field sensitivity. This work demonstrates a pathway to integrate quantum sensing with solid-state magnonics for practical quantum technology.
main_problem: To develop a highly sensitive, chip-scale quantum magnetometer by coupling Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) center ensembles to a passive magnonic cavity.
main_result: The projected sensitivity reaches 72 pT/$\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$ by combining the three hyperfine-resolved edges, representing a significant enhancement over single-resonance measurements.
method: The system dynamics are modeled using a Tavis-Cummings Hamiltonian coupled to a Lindblad master equation, analyzed via both ODMR and homodyne readout techniques.
model_or_system: The platform uses a 1D YIG/CoFeB magnonic crystal with a structural defect creating a passive cavity mode. NV ensembles are coupled to this mode, which is biased by integrated permanent magnets.
key_observables: Hyperfine-resolved optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) spectrum and dispersive homodyne response ($\text{Re}\langle a \rangle$).
important_parameters: Optimal coupling strength ratio ($g_{\text{ens}}/2\pi \approx 0.2$-$0.4 \text{ MHz}$); thermal limits (e.g., 1.7 pT/$\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$).
main_assumptions: The sensitivity calculation relies on combining independent estimates in quadrature and assumes the system operates in a regime where the coupling is strong enough to yield measurable spectral features.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the band structure showing the defect-localized mode, the local dipolar field profile at the NV site, and the resulting ODMR/homodyne spectra showing multiple steep edges.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from characterizing the magnonic cavity mode via micromagnetics to developing the coupled quantum model (Tavis-Cummings/Lindblad) and finally calculating the enhanced sensitivity using both ODMR and homodyne readout formalisms.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it combines cavity QED principles (cavity enhancement, coupling to quantum emitters) with solid-state magnonics, providing a roadmap for next-generation quantum sensors.

Spintronics.note: The paper directly models the coupling between quantum emitters (NV centers) and a magnonic cavity mode using a Tavis-Cummings Hamiltonian, which is a direct extension of cavity QED physics applied to magnons/spin waves.
